guide.seoTitle: ZYTO Scan: What It Is and {n} Practitioners to Book
guide.seoDescription: What a ZYTO scan is, how the hand cradle works, what the FDA has and has not cleared, and {n} ZYTO practitioners ranked by rating and reviews.

sections.h: What is a ZYTO scan?
p: A ZYTO scan is a session on a system made by ZYTO Technologies, a company based in Lindon, Utah. The client rests one hand on the ZYTO hand cradle, a small device with contact points for the fingertips and palm. The cradle passes a very small electrical current through the skin and records how easily it flows. That reading is called galvanic skin response, or GSR.

While the hand rests on the cradle, the ZYTO software shows a series of on-screen items and logs the skin response to each one. ZYTO calls them virtual items and calls the whole process biocommunication. Those terms are the company's own. They do not name an established scientific method.

sections.h: What happens in a ZYTO session
p: Most sessions follow the same pattern. A short conversation about what the client wants from the session, a few minutes with one hand on the cradle while the scan runs on the practitioner's computer, then a walk through the report. The practitioner usually talks about lifestyle, nutrition or wellness products in light of that report. Practitioners name several ZYTO systems, among them Select, Elite, Balance and Evox, and a session can look different on each one.

Some practitioners on ScannerFinder also run sessions at a distance. Before you book, ask whether you need to be there in person, how long the session takes, what it costs and whether any products are sold afterwards.

sections.h: What the FDA has cleared, and what it has not
p: The FDA cleared the ZYTO Hand Cradle in August 2011 (510(k) K111308) as a Class II device for one use: measuring galvanic skin response. The clearance covers that measurement and nothing more.

The FDA sent ZYTO Technologies warning letters in May 2015 and June 2023. The 2023 letter said the company was again promoting the device beyond that clearance, including linking scan results to named conditions, and that it had not validated the device or its software for those claims. So read a ZYTO session as a wellness session. It is not a medical test, and a scan report is no basis for health decisions. Talk to a licensed healthcare professional about any health concern.

sections.h: What the evidence does not show
p: We found no peer-reviewed study showing that ZYTO readings can be used to choose supplements or to judge someone's health. Skin response changes with sweat, skin moisture and how firmly the hand rests on the cradle, which is one reason independent reviewers such as Science-Based Medicine have criticised scanning built on it.

sections.h: How to choose a ZYTO practitioner
p: The {n} ZYTO practitioners listed here are mostly wellness centers, chiropractors, naturopathic practitioners and health consultants, and a few are supplement shops. Three questions are worth asking on the first call: which ZYTO system they use, what the session includes and costs, and whether you are expected to buy products after the scan. A practice that answers all three plainly is a good place to start.

faqs.q: What is a ZYTO scan?
faqs.a: A ZYTO scan is a wellness session in which the client rests a hand on the ZYTO hand cradle while software records galvanic skin response, a measure of how easily a tiny electrical current passes through the skin, against a series of on-screen items.

faqs.q: Is the ZYTO hand cradle FDA approved?
faqs.a: The FDA cleared the ZYTO Hand Cradle in 2011 (K111308) only to measure galvanic skin response. It has not cleared it for anything beyond that measurement, and it sent the company warning letters in 2015 and 2023 for promoting it for other uses.

faqs.q: How much does a ZYTO scan cost?
faqs.a: Each practice sets its own price, and ScannerFinder shows a price only once the practitioner confirms it. Ask on the phone what the session includes, how long it lasts and whether products are sold afterwards.

sources.label: FDA warning letter to ZYTO Technologies, 21 June 2023

guide.seoTitle: BICOM Bioresonance: What It Is and {n} Practitioners to Book
guide.seoDescription: What BICOM bioresonance is, who makes it, how a session works, what regulators in the UK and Australia have said, and {n} BICOM practitioners ranked by rating.

sections.h: What is BICOM bioresonance?
p: BICOM is a bioresonance device made by Regumed in Germany. It grew out of the MORA method that the physician Franz Morell and the engineer Erich Rasche developed in 1977. The client is connected through hand electrodes or applicators. According to the maker and its users, the device picks up the body's own oscillations, changes them by amplifying, weakening or inverting them, and sends them back.
That is how the method is described by those who sell and use it. A BICOM practice handbook itself says the method rests on years of experience rather than on generally accepted science.

sections.h: What happens in a BICOM session
p: A session usually has two parts. First a test phase, in which the practitioner works through the device's programs. Then a balancing phase, in which the device is said to send adjusted signals back through the electrodes or applicators. Ask how many sessions the practitioner expects and what they cost in total before you start.

sections.h: What regulators have said
p: In the United Kingdom, the Advertising Standards Authority has upheld complaints against bioresonance advertisers, including Bicom UK LLP and clinics using the method. In one 2018 ruling it said that a device being CE marked did not on its own show that it worked. In Australia, according to the group Friends of Science in Medicine, the last bioresonance devices were removed from the national register of therapeutic goods in 2020.

sections.h: What the evidence does not show
p: The best-known controlled trial of bioresonance, in children with eczema in 1997, found no effect beyond sham sessions. We found no independent study showing that BICOM readings are meaningful. Read a BICOM session as a wellness session, not a medical test, and talk to a licensed healthcare professional about any health concern.

sections.h: How to choose a BICOM practitioner
p: Ask which BICOM model they use, whether they trained with the maker, how many sessions they expect, and what the full course costs. The {n} BICOM practitioners listed here are ranked by Google rating weighted by review count.

faqs.q: What is BICOM bioresonance?
faqs.a: BICOM is a bioresonance device made by Regumed in Germany. Its makers say it picks up the body's own oscillations, changes them and sends them back through electrodes. There is no accepted scientific evidence that it does.

faqs.q: Who makes BICOM?
faqs.a: BICOM devices are made by Regumed, a German company. The method grew out of the MORA bioresonance work of Franz Morell and Erich Rasche in 1977.

faqs.q: Is BICOM an approved medical device?
faqs.a: Being registered or CE marked is not evidence that a device works, as the UK Advertising Standards Authority has pointed out. No regulator has accepted BICOM as a way to assess health.

faqs.q: How much does a BICOM session cost?
faqs.a: Each practice sets its own price, and ScannerFinder shows a price only once the practitioner confirms it. Ask on the phone what the session includes, how long it lasts and whether products are sold afterwards.

guide.seoTitle: Asyra and QEST4 Scan: What It Is and {n} Practitioners to Book
guide.seoDescription: What an Asyra or QEST4 scan is, how a session works, what is and is not established about it, and {n} Asyra practitioners ranked by rating and reviews.

sections.h: What is an Asyra scan?
p: Asyra is a computer-based scanning system, and its current version is sold as QEST4. In a session the client holds hand electrodes connected to the device while the software works through a long list of items, and the system records the body's electrical response to each one.

Critics describe it as a galvanic skin response device: it measures how easily a very small current passes through the skin. Sellers describe it differently, as presenting questions to the body through signals and reading the answers. That is the seller's account, not a tested mechanism.

sections.h: What happens in an Asyra session
p: A typical session starts with a conversation, then a few minutes with the hand electrodes while the scan runs on the practitioner's screen. The report groups its results by body system, and the practitioner usually talks about lifestyle, nutrition or wellness products in light of it.
Asyra is one of the devices named most often by practitioners on ScannerFinder who also offer remote sessions. The standard scan needs hand contact, so ask how a remote session works before you book.

sections.h: Regulatory status
p: Critics report that the Asyra was cleared by the FDA in 2003 only for measuring galvanic skin resistance. We could not confirm that clearance in the FDA's database. Either way, no regulator has accepted the Asyra or QEST4 as a way to assess health. Read a session as a wellness session, not a medical test, and talk to a licensed healthcare professional about any health concern.

sections.h: What the evidence does not show
p: We found no peer-reviewed study showing that Asyra readings are repeatable or that they can be used to judge someone's health. Skin response changes with sweat, skin moisture and how the electrodes are held, which is the main reason scientists doubt scanning built on it. The page on whether bioresonance works covers the research in more detail.

sections.h: How to choose an Asyra practitioner
p: Ask which version they use (Asyra Pro or QEST4), what the session includes and costs, and whether you are expected to buy products after the scan. The {n} Asyra practitioners listed here are ranked by Google rating weighted by review count.

faqs.q: What is an Asyra scan?
faqs.a: An Asyra scan is a wellness session in which the client holds hand electrodes while software records the body's electrical response to a long list of items. Critics describe it as a galvanic skin response device.

faqs.q: Is QEST4 the same as Asyra?
faqs.a: QEST4 is the current generation of the Asyra system, and practitioners use both names. Ask which version a practice uses.

faqs.q: Does the Asyra machine really work?
faqs.a: No study has shown that its readings are repeatable or accurate as a way to assess health, and no regulator has accepted it for that. Treat a session as a wellness session.

faqs.q: How much does an Asyra session cost?
faqs.a: Each practice sets its own price, and ScannerFinder shows a price only once the practitioner confirms it. Ask on the phone what the session includes, how long it lasts and whether products are sold afterwards.

guide.seoTitle: NES Health Scan: What It Is and {n} Practitioners to Book
guide.seoDescription: What an NES Health body-field scan is, how it relates to Energy4Life, miHealth and Infoceuticals, what the evidence shows, and {n} NES Health practitioners.

sections.h: What is an NES Health scan?
p: NES Health, short for Nutri-Energetics Systems, was set up in the early 2000s by the Australian researcher Peter Fraser and the British entrepreneur Harry Massey. Its scan is described as a reading of the human body-field, an energy field the company says surrounds and organises the body. The company now trades as Energy4Life, and neshealth.com redirects there.

The scan is a software program, and the company describes a version that runs from a short voice recording. The idea of a body-field that can be read this way is the company's own. It is not an established scientific concept.

sections.h: miHealth and Infoceuticals
p: NES practitioners often work with two other products from the same company. miHealth is a handheld device that the company describes as combining several kinds of electrical and magnetic stimulation with its own signals. Infoceuticals are liquid drops that the company says carry encoded information. A practitioner may suggest either one after a scan.

sections.h: What happens in an NES session
p: Many NES practitioners work at a distance, because the scan does not need the client in the room. A session usually covers the scan, a walk through the report, and suggestions for lifestyle, miHealth sessions or Infoceuticals. Ask before you book whether products are part of the plan and what they cost.

sections.h: What the evidence does not show
p: The company points to its own research. We found no independent peer-reviewed study showing that the scan reads anything meaningful about the body. Science-Based Medicine has criticised the model of scanning the body-field and then selling products to correct what the scan finds. No regulator has accepted the scan as a way to assess health, so read a session as a wellness session and talk to a licensed healthcare professional about any health concern.

sections.h: How to choose an NES Health practitioner
p: Ask whether the session is in person or remote, which NES or Energy4Life products they use, and whether a package of Infoceuticals or miHealth sessions is expected. The {n} NES Health practitioners listed here are ranked by Google rating weighted by review count.

faqs.q: What is an NES Health scan?
faqs.a: It is a wellness scan that the company describes as a reading of the human body-field. It runs as software and can be done from a short voice recording, so many sessions are remote.

faqs.q: Is NES Health the same as Energy4Life?
faqs.a: Yes. NES Health now trades as Energy4Life, and neshealth.com redirects to the Energy4Life site. Practitioners may use either name.

faqs.q: What are Infoceuticals?
faqs.a: Infoceuticals are liquid drops sold by NES Health that the company says carry encoded information. There is no independent evidence that they do anything specific.

faqs.q: How much does an NES Health session cost?
faqs.a: Each practice sets its own price, and ScannerFinder shows a price only once the practitioner confirms it. Ask on the phone what the session includes, how long it lasts and whether products are sold afterwards.

sections.h: What is Rayonex bioresonance?
p: Rayonex Biomedical is a German company based in Lennestadt, founded in 1982. Its method is called bioresonance according to Paul Schmidt, after the engineer who founded the company. The company describes it as working with frequencies applied to the body through electrodes or applicators.

The main devices are the Rayocomp PS 1000 polar, used in practices, and the smaller Rayocomp PS 10, which is also sold for use at home. That makes Rayonex one of the few brands that clients can buy for themselves.

sections.h: Device class in the EU

A device class describes how a product is regulated and made. It does not show that the method works for any purpose that a seller or practitioner advertises.

sections.h: What the evidence does not show

That study is published or promoted by the company, and we found no independent trial that confirms it. More broadly, controlled research on bioresonance has not found an effect beyond placebo. Read a Rayonex session as a wellness session, not a medical test, and talk to a licensed healthcare professional about any health concern.

guide.seoTitle: NLS Scan (Metatron, Oberon): What It Is and {n} Practitioners
guide.seoDescription: What an NLS scan with a Metatron or Oberon device is, how a session works, where the devices come from, what the evidence shows, and {n} NLS practitioners.

sections.h: What is an NLS scan?
p: NLS stands for non-linear system, a scanning method that began in Russia. The best-known developer is the Institute of Practical Psychophysics in Omsk, founded in 1990, and devices are sold under names such as Oberon, Metatron and Hunter 4025. In a session the client wears headphones with built-in sensors while a computer runs the scan and shows images of organs and body systems on screen.
The sellers describe the device as reading the magnetic field of the body and comparing it with stored patterns. No published research shows that a device can do this.

sections.h: Where the devices come from
p: Original Russian systems are sold alongside many copies. Many of the Metatron Hunter 4025 devices sold on online marketplaces are made in China, and public prices run from a few hundred to a few thousand dollars. A low device price is one reason NLS scans are common in small practices.

sections.h: What happens in an NLS session
p: The client sits with the headphones on for the scan, which runs through body systems one by one on the practitioner's screen. Some practitioners follow the scan with a balancing program on the same device. Many NLS practitioners on ScannerFinder also offer remote sessions; ask how a remote session works, since the standard scan needs the headphones.

sections.h: What the evidence does not show
p: We found no independent peer-reviewed study showing that NLS scans are accurate or repeatable. The images on screen are produced by software and do not show your own organs. Read a session as a wellness session, not a medical test, and talk to a licensed healthcare professional about any health concern.

sections.h: How to choose an NLS practitioner
p: Ask which device they use (Oberon, Metatron or another NLS system), what the session includes and costs, and whether you are expected to buy products. The {n} NLS practitioners listed here are ranked by Google rating weighted by review count.

faqs.q: What is an NLS scan?
faqs.a: An NLS (non-linear system) scan is a wellness session in which the client wears headphones with sensors while software runs a scan and shows images of body systems. The method began in Russia.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Metatron and Oberon?
faqs.a: Both are names for NLS scanning devices. Oberon is associated with the original Russian systems, and many Metatron Hunter 4025 devices sold online are lower-cost copies.

faqs.q: Does an NLS scan show my organs?
faqs.a: No. The images on screen are generated by the software. They are not imaging of your body, and no study has shown the scan reads anything meaningful.

faqs.q: How much does an NLS session cost?
faqs.a: Each practice sets its own price, and ScannerFinder shows a price only once the practitioner confirms it. Ask on the phone what the session includes, how long it lasts and whether products are sold afterwards.

guide.seoTitle: SCIO, Indigo and Eductor Biofeedback: What It Is and {n} Practitioners
guide.seoDescription: What SCIO, Indigo and Eductor biofeedback is, where the devices come from, their FDA history, what the evidence shows, and {n} practitioners ranked by rating.

sections.h: What are SCIO, Indigo and Eductor?
p: SCIO, Indigo and Eductor are generations of one family of devices that began in the 1980s as the EPFX, also sold as the QXCI. The client is linked to the device through electrodes, usually on the wrists, ankles and forehead, and software runs through a large library of frequencies. According to the sellers, the device reads the body's reactions to those frequencies and sends others back.

That is the sellers' account. Critics class the device as radionics, a method with no basis in physics. Practitioners sell sessions under names such as quantum biofeedback, SCIO biofeedback or Indigo biofeedback.

sections.h: Where the devices come from
p: The original device was invented by William Nelson, who registered his company with the FDA in 1989 as a maker of biofeedback machines, a category that allows sales only as a relaxation or stress tool. In 1992 the FDA warned him over claims that went far beyond that. In 1996 he was indicted in the United States on fraud charges and moved to Budapest, where the devices continued to be made.

In 2004 a Seattle Times investigation reported cases of people who had relied on the device instead of medical care. The FDA then opened a compliance investigation and issued an import alert against new shipments. The SCIO has since been discontinued in favour of newer models, and used systems are still sold.

sections.h: What happens in a session
p: In a session the client sits or lies down with the electrodes on, the software runs a scan, and the practitioner then runs programs that the device is said to use to balance the body. Many SCIO and Indigo practitioners also offer remote sessions and sessions for animals. Ask how those work before you book.

sections.h: What the evidence does not show
p: We found no peer-reviewed study showing that SCIO, Indigo or Eductor readings are accurate or repeatable, or that the programs do anything beyond a relaxing appointment. Read a session as a wellness session, not a medical test, and talk to a licensed healthcare professional about any health concern.

sections.h: How to choose a practitioner
p: Ask which device and software version they use, how long a session lasts, what a full course costs, and whether you are expected to buy products. The {n} practitioners listed here are ranked by Google rating weighted by review count.

faqs.q: What is SCIO biofeedback?
faqs.a: SCIO is a device from the EPFX and QXCI family. The client is linked to it through electrodes while software runs through a library of frequencies. Its sellers say it reads the body's reactions and sends back balancing frequencies; critics class it as radionics.

faqs.q: Is Indigo the same as SCIO?
faqs.a: Indigo and Eductor are later devices in the same family as the SCIO, which has been discontinued. Practitioners often use the names interchangeably.

faqs.q: Is SCIO FDA approved?
faqs.a: No. The maker registered it as a biofeedback device for relaxation only, the FDA warned against wider claims in 1992, and in 2004 it issued an import alert against new shipments.

faqs.q: How much does a SCIO or Indigo session cost?
faqs.a: Each practice sets its own price, and ScannerFinder shows a price only once the practitioner confirms it. Ask on the phone what the session includes, how long it lasts and whether products are sold afterwards.

sources.label: Seattle Times, FDA and Congress act (2004)

guide.seoTitle: MORA Bioresonance: What It Is and {n} Practitioners to Book
guide.seoDescription: What MORA bioresonance is, the 1977 origin of the method, who makes MORA devices today, what the evidence shows, and {n} MORA practitioners ranked by rating.

sections.h: What is MORA bioresonance?
p: MORA is the original bioresonance method. It was developed in Germany in 1977, and its name comes from the first letters of the surnames of the physician Franz Morell and the engineer Erich Rasche. Later bioresonance devices, including BICOM, grew out of the same work.

MORA devices are made today by Med-Tronik, a German company that holds the MORA trademarks, including the current MORA-Nova. The client is connected through hand electrodes or applicators, and according to its makers the device picks up the body's oscillations and sends adjusted ones back.

sections.h: What happens in a MORA session
p: A session usually combines a test phase and a balancing phase with the device, often over a series of appointments. MORA is one of the least common devices in this directory: {n} practitioners, spread across several countries. Ask how many sessions they expect and what the full course costs.

sections.h: What the evidence does not show
p: Controlled research on bioresonance has not found an effect beyond placebo, and we found no independent study of MORA devices that shows otherwise. Med-Tronik describes the method as free of side effects; that is the maker's claim, not an independent finding. Read a session as a wellness session, not a medical test, and talk to a licensed healthcare professional about any health concern.

sections.h: How to choose a MORA practitioner
p: Ask which MORA device they use, whether they trained with the maker, how many sessions they expect, and what the full course costs. The {n} MORA practitioners listed here are ranked by Google rating weighted by review count.

faqs.q: What is MORA therapy?
faqs.a: MORA is the original bioresonance method, developed in Germany in 1977 by Franz Morell and Erich Rasche. Its name comes from their surnames. There is no accepted scientific evidence that it works.

faqs.q: Who makes MORA devices?
faqs.a: MORA devices, including the MORA-Nova, are made by Med-Tronik, a German company that holds the MORA trademarks.

faqs.q: Is MORA the same as BICOM?
faqs.a: They share the same roots. BICOM grew out of the MORA work of 1977, but the two are made by different companies.

faqs.a: Each practice sets its own price, and ScannerFinder shows a price only once the practitioner confirms it. Ask on the phone what the session includes, how long it lasts and whether products are sold afterwards.

guide.seoTitle: AO Scan: What It Is and {n} Practitioners to Book
guide.seoDescription: What an AO Scan session is, how the Inner Voice, Vitals and Comprehensive scans are described, its regulatory status, and {n} AO Scan practitioners ranked by rating.

sections.h: What is an AO Scan?
p: AO Scan is a wellness technology sold by the company Solex. It runs through the AO Scan app, and practitioners and individuals use it on a monthly subscription. The seller and its distributors describe it in terms of frequencies: the scan is said to compare the body against a library of frequency signatures and to play back balancing frequencies.
Those descriptions come from the seller. Words such as quantum resonance and scalar waves appear in AO Scan material, but they do not describe how the device works in any way that has been tested.

sections.h: The three AO Scans
p: Inner Voice records a short voice sample and plays back a sound built from it. Practitioners use it in relaxation and focus sessions, and it is one reason some AO Scan sessions run from a voice recording alone.
Vitals and Comprehensive produce reports. Comprehensive covers a long list of organs and body systems and scores each one on a scale of 1 to 9, where 5 is described as balanced.

sections.h: Regulatory status
p: We could not find an FDA clearance for the AO Scan. Distributor materials state that AO Scan Technology is not a medical device and that its statements have not been evaluated by the FDA. ScannerFinder lists AO Scan sessions on the same terms: as wellness sessions, not medical tests. Talk to a licensed healthcare professional about any health concern.

sections.h: What the evidence does not show
p: We found no peer-reviewed study of the AO Scan. Scientists and physicians who have looked at biofrequency devices of this kind, such as the authors of the NeuroLogica blog, describe their claims as unsupported.

sections.h: AO Scan or ZYTO?
p: Both are wellness scans, and they work differently. ZYTO records skin response through a hand cradle, and the FDA has cleared that cradle to measure skin response and nothing more. AO Scan is app-based, is described in terms of frequencies and has no FDA clearance. Remote sessions are more common with AO Scan, and a few practices on ScannerFinder use both.

sections.h: How to choose an AO Scan practitioner
p: AO Scan is also sold through distributors, and some practitioners are distributors as well. So ask on the first call whether the session comes with a subscription or product offer. Also ask whether you need to attend in person, which scans the session includes and what it costs.

faqs.q: What is an AO Scan?
faqs.a: An AO Scan is a wellness session run through the AO Scan app from Solex. The seller describes it in terms of frequencies, and its three scans are Inner Voice, Vitals and Comprehensive.

faqs.q: Is the AO Scan FDA approved?
faqs.a: We could not find an FDA clearance for the AO Scan. Distributor materials state that it is not a medical device and that its statements have not been evaluated by the FDA.

faqs.q: What is the AO Scan Inner Voice?
faqs.a: Inner Voice records a short voice sample and plays back a sound built from it. Practitioners use it in relaxation and focus sessions, and it can be run from a recording.

faqs.q: How much does an AO Scan session cost?
faqs.a: Each practice sets its own price, and ScannerFinder shows a price only once the practitioner confirms it. Ask on the phone what the session includes, how long it lasts and whether products are sold afterwards.
